back: A single-team process framework for product development, made of roles, events, artifacts and rules, delivering working product in sprints.
A timebox of one month or less, of consistent length, in which a potentially releasable increment is produced.
Product owner, development team, scrum master.
Sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective.
Product backlog, sprint backlog, increment.
Responsible for maximizing the value of the product. Owns and orders the product backlog. Accepts or declines finished work.
A cross-functional, self-organizing team with all the skills needed to deliver the working product. Decides how to do the work.
A servant leader who makes sure the Scrum process is followed, coaches the team and removes impediments. Does not assign tasks.
The team has all the skills needed to produce the working product without depending on people outside the team.
Team members decide how to do the work, share ownership of the outcome and adjust roles as needed.
The ordered list of all the work for the product. Owned by the product owner; never finished.
The items the team selected for the current sprint, plus its plan for delivering them.
The finished, usable work produced in a sprint, added to all earlier increments.
Opens the sprint. The product owner presents priorities; the team decides how much it can take on, based on its capacity.
A meeting of at most 15 minutes for the team to coordinate. Three questions: completed, planned, impediments. Not a status meeting; no problem-solving.
The team demonstrates the working increment to stakeholders and gets feedback. Inspects the product.
The team looks at how it worked and chooses a few improvements. Inspects the process. Last event of the sprint; not about blame.
Review: the product, with stakeholders. Retrospective: the process, within the team.
Preparing stories for upcoming sprints: clarifying, splitting and estimating. Usually mid-sprint, led by the product owner with the team.
The team's shared checklist of what an increment must meet to be finished: integrated, tested, compliant, documented, accepted.
What a backlog item needs before the team will take it into a sprint.
A fixed maximum period of time. When it ends, the event or sprint ends.
Where problems raised in the daily scrum are noted, to be solved afterwards by the people involved.
Transparency, inspection, adaptation.
Commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage.

front: Who decides how much work goes into a sprint?
back: The development team, based on its capacity.

front: A stakeholder wants a new feature mid-sprint. Where does it go?
back: To the product owner, who adds it to the product backlog and prioritizes it. Not straight into the sprint.

front: Unfinished work at the end of a sprint
back: It is not counted or demonstrated as done. It returns to the product backlog. The sprint is not extended.

front: Is there a project manager in Scrum?
back: No. The duties are shared among the product owner (scope, priorities), the team (its own work) and the scrum master (the process).
A short piece of research done to understand an unknown or a risk before committing to an item.
